name: Stakeholder Buy-In
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Turning Skeptics Into Champions: The Practice of Stakeholder Buy-In
lesson.summary: Buy-in is the active, ongoing work of converting a stakeholder map into genuine support, built by answering "what's in it for me" for each group and sequencing early wins before asking for the harder commitments.
lesson.body:
Stakeholder analysis produces a map: who has power, who has interest, who is affected by a proposed system. That map is diagnostic, not persuasive. Knowing that the finance director has high power and currently low interest tells you where a problem is likely to surface. It does nothing, by itself, to fix it. Buy-in is the deliberate, ongoing work of converting that map into actual support, and it is a distinct skill from the analysis that precedes it.

The starting question for every stakeholder group is the same one, even though the honest answer differs group by group: what's in it for me. A procurement team evaluating a blockchain-based supplier verification system does not care, in the first instance, about disintermediation or cryptographic trust minimization, concepts that may have motivated the project's architects. They care about whether onboarding a new supplier will take less time, whether disputes will be easier to resolve, and whether the new system will make their monthly reporting harder or easier. A buy-in effort that leads with the technology's elegance rather than each group's own stake in the outcome is optimizing for the wrong audience, and it is one of the most common ways technically sound blockchain projects lose the room.

Sequencing matters as much as messaging. The change management chapter's emphasis on early wins applies directly here: asking a skeptical business unit for a large, risky commitment before it has seen any evidence the system works is a much harder sell than asking a smaller, more receptive group to run a narrow pilot first, and then bringing the skeptics visible proof rather than a promise. This is also why executive sponsorship matters disproportionately. A credible senior sponsor does not just approve budget; they signal to the rest of the organization that resistance carries a cost and that support carries visible backing, which changes the calculus for stakeholders who are privately undecided.

Buy-in earned early is not a one-time achievement, either. Support tends to erode across a long project timeline, particularly through the gap between a promising proof of concept and a scaled pilot, a stretch covered later in this course precisely because organizational patience often runs out before technical value is demonstrated at scale. Champions identified early, people with credibility in their own part of the organization who genuinely believe in the project, need to be given visible ownership and kept informed as the project evolves, not simply recruited once and then left to advocate from stale information. A stakeholder converted to a champion during the proof of concept phase is one of the strongest assets a consortium or organization has when it later needs to defend a pilot's continuation against the inevitable, and often reasonable, questions about cost and risk.
